Guitar · structured development

Chord Training

A practical route from clean chord formation to fluent, musical chord playing. Open any step whenever you need a reminder of what to practise and how to do it.

6 training disciplines180-minute full sessionTechnique + harmony
TRAINING STEPS
REFERENCE
STEP 01 · FOUNDATION

Chord formation

Make every chord clean before trying to play it quickly.

Exercise: Form · play · release · repeat

Start with C, G, D, Am and Em. Work on one chord at a time.

  1. Form the chord slowly.
  2. Place each fingertip close behind its fret without touching it.
  3. Pick each string individually and listen for buzzes, muted notes or unwanted noise.
  4. Correct the shape until every intended note rings clearly.
  5. Release your fretting hand completely, then form the chord again.
  6. When comfortable, repeat without looking at your fretting hand.
20 repetitionsper chord

Progression drill

Form the chord, lift your fingers about 1 cm off the strings, then reform it. Keep the hand relaxed and avoid letting the shape collapse between repetitions.

STEP 02 · FRETTING-HAND ECONOMY

Chord transitions

Build repeatable movement between chord shapes without losing the pulse.

Exercise: Two-chord transitions

Use these pairs: C → G · G → D · D → Am · Am → Em · Em → C.

  1. Form the first chord.
  2. Strum four even beats.
  3. Move to the second chord and strum four even beats.
  4. Repeat the pair continuously, keeping the tempo steady.
  5. Practise the reverse direction as a separate movement.
2 minutesper chord pair · 50–60 BPM

What to look for

  • Fingers that can stay anchored.
  • Fingers that can move together.
  • Small adjustments instead of lifting and replacing the whole hand.
  • The shortest comfortable path between shapes.

Only increase the speed after the changes are clean and consistent.

STEP 03 · HAND SYNCHRONIZATION

Silent chord coordination

Remove the picking-hand distraction and train the fretting hand to move as a coordinated unit.

Exercise: Change chords without strumming

Use this sequence: C → Am → F → G → C.

  1. Form C and pause briefly.
  2. Move to Am without playing the strings.
  3. Continue to F, G and back to C.
  4. Repeat slowly, aiming for smooth, simultaneous finger placement.
  5. Gradually reduce the pause between shapes without adding tension.
5–10 minutescontinuous slow practice

Check each movement

  • No unnecessary finger travel.
  • No collapsing wrist or excessive tension.
  • Consistent fingertip placement.
  • Minimal time between one shape releasing and the next shape landing.
STEP 04 · FRETBOARD FLUENCY

Triads and inversions

Learn to find and connect chord tones across the neck rather than relying only on full six-string shapes.

Reference chord: C major = C · E · G
Root positionC – E – G
First inversionE – G – C
Second inversionG – C – E

Work across all four string sets

123234345456
  1. Find C major root position on a string set.
  2. Find its first inversion, then its second inversion.
  3. Play each shape individually and identify the root, third and fifth.
  4. Move between the three inversions without stopping.
  5. Repeat with Dm, Em, F, G, Am and Bdim.

Keep the note spellings clear: the inversion changes which chord tone is lowest, not which notes belong to the chord.

STEP 05 · HARMONIC CONNECTION

Voice leading

Connect chords by moving each voice the smallest practical distance.

Progression: C → Am → F → G → C

Use nearby inversions instead of jumping to unrelated positions. Keep the chords in the same general register and listen to how each note moves as the harmony changes.

C majorC – E – G
A minorA – C – E
F majorA – C – F
G majorG – B – D
  1. Choose a string set and find a playable C triad.
  2. Find the nearest inversion of Am.
  3. Continue to the nearest F and G triads.
  4. Return to C with the smallest practical movement.
  5. Repeat on the other string sets.

Listen for common tones that stay in place and chord tones that move by a step. This is the foundation for hearing harmonic movement, tension and release.

STEP 06 · PERFORMANCE

Rhythm and strumming

Keep the pulse even while changing chords, and learn to control dynamics and accents.

Use the progression C → Am → F → G. Start at 60 BPM.

Pattern 1Four downstrokes
Pattern 2Down – up – down – up
Pattern 3Down – down-up – up-down-up
Pattern 4Continuous eighth notes
Pattern 5Muted strumming with chord changes

Tempo ladder

60 BPM80 BPM100 BPM120 BPM

Move up the tempo ladder only while the rhythm remains even. Practise quietly, loudly and with accents on different beats. Keep the pulse steady regardless of the chord.

REFERENCE · 180 MINUTES

Three-hour training session

A balanced session that develops technique, fretboard knowledge, harmony and musical application.

25 min
Chord formation

Clean fretting, individual strings and repeated formations.

30 min
Chord transitions

Two-chord changes, metronome and finger efficiency.

20 min
Chord coordination

Silent chord changes and synchronized finger movement.

35 min
Triads and inversions

All four string sets, three inversions and chord recognition.

30 min
Voice leading

Diatonic progressions and minimum-distance movement.

25 min
Rhythm and strumming

Timing, accents, dynamics and rhythmic patterns.

15 min
Musical application

Play complete progressions and create your own combinations.

Take short breaks between blocks. Three hours of focused practice is better than three hours of repetitive, fatigued playing.

REFERENCE · NON-NEGOTIABLES

Practice standards

Use these rules throughout every training block.

  1. Never accept a dirty chord.If a note buzzes or is muted unintentionally, correct it before continuing.
  2. Never practise speed before accuracy.Speed develops from efficient, repeatable movements.
  3. Practise both directions.C → G and G → C are separate movements worth practising.
  4. Practise without looking occasionally.Your fingers need to develop spatial awareness.
  5. Always connect technique to music.Every exercise should eventually become part of a progression or musical phrase.

Long-term targets

  • Play major, minor, diminished, augmented and suspended chords.
  • Find all three triad inversions anywhere on the neck.
  • Change chords while maintaining a steady rhythm.
  • Harmonize a major key.
  • Play progressions horizontally rather than relying only on CAGED positions.
  • Understand why chords create tension and how they resolve.
